Das Vortragende präsentiert "LayoutMask", ein neues Modell zur Verbesserung der Text-Layout-Interaktion in multi-modalen Vortrainingsmodellen für Dokumentenverstehen. Ziel ist es, die Lesereihenfolgeprobleme in visuell reichen Dokumenten zu adressieren. LayoutMask verwendet lokale 1D-Positionen anstelle von globalen Positionen und integriert innovative Maskierungsstrategien und Vortrainingsoptimierungen, um die Interaktion zwischen Text und Layout zu verbessern. Die Methodologie kombiniert Maskierte Sprachmodellierung und Maskierte Positionsmodellierung, wobei die Token-Einbettung, die lokale und segmentale 2D-Position sowie die Maskierungsstrategie für Wörter und Boxen berücksichtigt werden. Experimentelle Ergebnisse zeigen, dass LayoutMask im Vergleich zu anderen Modellen wie FUNSD und CORD-19 höhere F1-Werte erreicht, insbesondere bei lokaler Segmentierung.

The presentation titled "Finding the SWEET spot: Analysis and Improvement of Adaptive Inference in Low Resource Settings" discusses strategies for optimizing machine learning models in resource-constrained environments. It highlights the variability in real-world data complexity, suggesting that low-capacity models can be used for simpler tasks to reduce inference costs. The talk compares two methods: Multi-Model (MM) and Early Exit (EE), noting that MM offers more versatility but is expensive to store and has overhead. EE, on the other hand, provides fast inference without overhead and is memory efficient, with shared model parameters across classifiers. The presentation introduces the hypothesis that conflicting gradients may degrade performance due to classifier optimization conflicts. It then presents results showing that Multi-Model models outperform Early Exit ones by 2.3% on average, with the largest gap observed for early classifiers. The SWEET method is introduced as a solution to separate weights in early exit transformers, avoiding conflicting gradients and improving performance. The final section summarizes key takeaways, including the existence of conflicting gradients in the training process, fair comparisons between EE and MM methods, and the potential for future research on fine-tuning algorithms tailored to the Early Exit architecture.

This research introduces a novel approach to multimodal relation extraction, focusing on the simultaneous subtraction and addition of information for enhanced performance. The method employs internal-information screening guided by the graph information bottleneck principle and latent multimodal topic modeling to enrich feature contexts. By integrating these techniques, the system achieves significant improvements over existing best models on benchmark data, demonstrating its effectiveness in handling mixed-modal inputs with varying text-image relevance. The study also explores the interplay between internal and external information, showing that while GENE excels under high text-image relevance, LAMO contributes more significantly when cross-modal feature relevance is low. This work underscores the importance of balancing internal and external information for optimal multimodal relation extraction.

Das Video präsentiert ein neues Ensemble-Learning-Framework namens LLM-Blender, das speziell für Large Language Models (LLMs) entwickelt wurde. Es kombiniert zwei Module: den PairRanker und den GenFuser. Der PairRanker nutzt Paarweise-Ranglistenverfahren, um die Leistung von LLMs zu verbessern, indem er Paare von Modellausgaben vergleicht und sie basierend auf ihrer Performance rankt. Der GenFuser fusioniert dann die besten Kandidaten aus dem PairRanker, um eine endgültige Antwort zu generieren. Die Präsentation behandelt die Herausforderungen und die Rolle von Prätrainingsdaten bei der Entwicklung von Sprachmodellen, insbesondere im Kontext politischer Biass und ihrer Auswirkungen auf die Fairness von NLP-Anwendungen.

Weitere Aspekte der Präsentation beinhalten Methoden zur Evaluierung der politischen Neigung von Sprachmodellen, wie das politische Kompass-Test und die Unterstützung sowohl für Encoder- als auch Decoder-Sprachmodelle. This research addresses the challenge of detecting cognitive dissonance, a rare class in text data, by leveraging transfer learning and active learning techniques. Cognitive dissonance refers to the discomfort experienced when two conflicting beliefs or actions are present within an individual's thought process. The study introduces a novel approach that combines transfer learning with active learning to efficiently annotate rare classes, such as cognitive dissonance, which are often underrepresented in datasets. By transferring knowledge from a related domain (e.g., debate texts) to the target domain (cognitive dissonance detection), the model is able to improve its performance on the rare class. Active learning strategies, including random sampling, entropy-based selection, core-set selection, and probability-of-rare-class (PRC) sampling, are evaluated for their effectiveness in annotating these rare classes. The results demonstrate that PRC sampling outperforms other strategies, achieving higher accuracy while requiring fewer annotations. This work not only advances the field of natural language processing but also provides practical insights into handling rare classes in complex domains like cognitive psychology.

This presentation explores the application of deep learning techniques to mathematical reasoning, focusing on various domains such as math word problems, geometry problem solving, automated theorem proving, and low-resource settings. It begins by introducing the 61st Annual Meeting of the Association for Computational Linguistics held in Toronto, Canada, setting the stage for discussions on computational linguistics and mathematics. The core of the presentation delves into how deep learning models can be used to solve complex mathematical problems, including arithmetic operations, geometry, and theorem proving. It highlights advancements in tools like Chameleon, which enable plug-and-play compositional reasoning using large language models (LLMs). The presentation also addresses challenges in generalization and robustness, demonstrating limitations in current LLMs when dealing with precise mathematical reasoning and large numbers. Additionally, it discusses the role of self-consistency in chain-of-thought prompting and the importance of program-aided LLMs for handling complex tasks. The final section covers low-resource settings, showcasing applications in fields like finance, science, and medicine, emphasizing the potential of LLMs in these areas despite their current limitations.

Das Video präsentiert ein Forschungsprojekt von Google Research, das sich mit der Aufgabe beschäftigt, indirekte Bezugnahme ausdrücke für die Auswahl von Entitäten zu lösen. Der Fokus liegt auf der Erstellung eines Korpus namens AltEntities, das 6.000 alternative Fragen und 42.000 indirekte Bezugnahme ausdrücke umfasst. Ziel ist es, die Sprachverarbeitung bei der Verständigung von Benutzern zu verbessern, insbesondere wenn sie ihre Wahl in natürlicher und flüssiger Konversation ausdrücken. Indirekte Bezugnahme ausdrücke können schwierig zu interpretieren sein, da sie oft den Namen einer Entität vergessen oder die Aussprache schwer zu unterscheiden sind. Das Projekt verwendet eine Methode zur Datensammlung, die auf einer Cartoon-Fertigstellungsaufgabe basiert, um Informalität zu betonen. Die Daten wurden durch Crowdsourcing gesammelt und drei verschiedene Domänen – Musik, Bücher und Rezepte – abgedeckt. The study's experiments across machine translation, language modeling, and abstractive summarization tasks show substantial improvements in BLEU scores and efficiency, validating the effectiveness of this approach.

The KITMUS Test is an evaluation framework designed to assess the ability of natural language understanding (NLU) models to integrate knowledge from multiple sources, both pretrain-time and inference-time. This study highlights that many NLU models struggle with reasoning over diverse knowledge types, indicating a need for task-specific training to enhance their performance. The presentation titled "Attention as a Guide for Simultaneous Speech Translation" by Sara Papi, Matteo Negri, and Marco Turchi explores the challenges and solutions in the field of simultaneous speech translation (SimuST). It begins by defining SimuST as the real-time translation of spoken language into text, enabling cross-language communication. The speakers highlight the problems with current SimuST models, such as the need for specific architectures, long training procedures, and the requirement to maintain multiple models for different latency regimes.
To address these issues, the solution proposed is EDAtt, an encoder-decoder attention mechanism that leverages existing offline ST models without retraining or adapting them specifically for SimuST. The approach uses only one model per latency regime and handles latency through specific parameters. By leveraging the attention mechanism between audio input and textual output, EDAtt decides whether to emit or not a partial translation based on where attention points, ensuring that the emitted word is stable and information-rich.
The study demonstrates that EDAtt outperforms all strategies applied to offline models, achieving state-of-the-art performance while being the fastest strategy when considering actual elapsed time. The results are supported by a detailed analysis of BLEU scores across various latency regimes, showcasing the effectiveness of the proposed method.

The presentation explores the potential of large language models (LLMs) as an alternative to human evaluations for assessing text quality. It begins with an overview of the topic, highlighting the method, related works, motivation, experiments, and open questions. The core idea is to use LLMs to rate texts by providing them with instructions and asking them to evaluate samples, which is referred to as "LLM evaluation." The presentation discusses the motivation behind this approach, noting that while the concept of using LLMs for evaluation seems natural and widely adopted, there were no prior works exploring this idea when the paper was submitted to ACL 2023.
The slide then delves into human evaluation, emphasizing its widespread adoption but also pointing out its instability and difficulty in reproducibility. It contrasts this with the proposed LLM evaluation method, suggesting it could offer a more consistent and scalable solution. The presentation outlines the experiment setting, where stories generated by GPT-2 and written by humans are rated by both LLMs and human evaluators using the same instructions. The four rating attributes considered are grammar, coherence, likeability, and relevance. The results show that larger LLMs (text-davinci-003 and ChatGPT) exhibit a clear preference for human-written stories, while smaller LLMs (T0: 13B and text-curie-001: 30B) do not show a meaningful preference. The final slides invite further discussion on the alignment between LLM responses and human ratings, the impact of instruction wording, and the broader implications of LLM evaluation compared to human evaluation.

The presentation discusses the importance of context in translation, emphasizing that translation often depends on the surrounding context. It highlights the challenges in evaluating context-dependent translations, noting that only a small portion of words rely on context and existing methods support limited discourse phenomena and languages. The study aims to identify when translation requires context and how well models handle these context-dependent translations. A key metric introduced is Conditional Cross-Mutual Information (CXMI), which measures the usage of context by machine translation models. The research also explores thematic analysis of high CXMI words, focusing on POS tags like pronouns and verb forms, as well as vocabulary items and individual tokens. The MuDA benchmark is used for model evaluation, showing that context-aware models perform better on some phenomena such as formality and lexical cohesion but struggle with ellipsis, pronouns, and verb forms. The study concludes with a dataset-agnostic benchmark for document-level machine translation, identifying discourse phenomena systematically without prior linguistic knowledge.

**Abstract**
This research introduces StoryTrans, an innovative approach for non-parallel story author-style transfer that leverages discourse representations and content enhancement techniques. The core challenge addressed is the imitation of authors' linguistic choices at the discourse level and the association of author styles with specific writing topics. To tackle these issues, the study proposes a two-step solution: first, it transfers discourse representations from the source to the target story, followed by enhancing the content to align with the target style. The proposed model utilizes an encoder-decoder architecture with a pointer network to maintain the original story's structure while adapting it to the desired style. The training framework employs a combination of language modeling and auto-encoder losses to ensure both style consistency and content preservation. Experimental results on Chinese and English datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of the method, achieving high style accuracy and content preservation scores. This work contributes significantly to the field of natural language processing, particularly in the area of authorial style transfer.

The presentation introduces FSUIE, a novel framework for enhancing Universal Information Extraction (UIE) tasks. It addresses the limitations of existing UIE models that heavily rely on precise span boundaries and mismatch between feature extraction and information extraction. FSUIE proposes a fuzzy span mechanism to model the boundary as a continuous distribution, improving the model's ability to handle ambiguity. The framework also utilizes efficient fuzzy span attention to adaptively adjust the attention span, guiding the proper distribution of attention. FSUIE achieves significant improvements over UIE-base models across various information extraction tasks, including Named Entity Recognition (NER), Relation Extraction (RE), and Argument Structure Extraction (ASTE). The model's performance is further enhanced by its unified extraction structure, which compares favorably with separate structures.

The presentation discusses the challenges of factual error correction (FEC) in dialogue summarization, where summaries generated by models often contain factual errors. It highlights two common approaches: directly designing better summarization models and using Factual Error Correction (FEC) models to correct model-generated summaries. The speaker explains that FEC models can be evaluated using factuality metrics like FactCC, which provide an overall score but may not be reliable on their own. The introduction of reference corrections is proposed as a solution, providing more valuable data for training FEC models compared to pseudo data and creating conditions for a more comprehensive evaluation of FEC model performance.

The presentation discusses the robustness of Natural Language Inference (NLI) models, focusing on minimizing shortcut learning. It introduces the concept of shortcuts as spurious correlations between input features and labels that can lead to poor generalization. The speaker highlights examples where models rely on these shortcuts rather than understanding the underlying logic. To mitigate this issue, the presentation outlines a minimax training approach, which aims to learn an example weight distribution emphasizing under-represented hard examples. This method is designed to improve out-of-distribution (OOD) performance while maintaining high in-distribution accuracy. The study explores various experiments, including the impact of pre-training, the size of the auxiliary model, and qualitative evaluations of the learned weights. The results show consistent improvements in OOD performance across different datasets, suggesting the effectiveness of the proposed method.

### Vergleich von prätrainierungsstrategien und Datenquellen
- **Evaluation der Auswirkungen von öffentlichen und privaten medizinischen Datenquellen auf vergleichbare Datengrößen** o **NACHOS**: Eine 1,18 Millionen Wörter offene Quellen-Datenbank mit heterogenen Daten aus verschiedenen medizinischen Domänen, natürlicher Sprache und stylerichtig. o **NBDW**: Eine private Datenbank von Sätzen, die aus 1,7 Millionen anonymisierten medizinischen Dokumenten der Nantes University Hospital Data Warehouse stammen.

The presentation discusses the concept of superhuman performance in natural language understanding (NLU) systems, emphasizing the challenges and limitations of current evaluation methods. It highlights that leaderboard-based evaluations have become popular but often lead to claims of superhuman capabilities, despite systems frequently achieving better-than-human performance on specific tasks. The SuperGLUE benchmark is introduced as a well-known framework for evaluating general-purpose language understanding models, listing various tasks such as Word in Context, Multi-Service Reading Comprehension, and Commitment Bank. The presentation also addresses the reliability of leaderboard scores by comparing them with human performance, noting that humans outperform systems on six out of ten SuperGLUE tasks. Additionally, it explores the issue of misleading comparisons between systems and humans, pointing out that these comparisons can be flawed due to differences in evaluation data, system performance, measurement processes, and human factors. The speaker concludes by discussing the consequences of these issues and providing recommendations for constructing fairer and more transparent benchmarks.

This research investigates the effectiveness of CoNLL-2003 named entity taggers in modern NER tasks, questioning whether models trained on this dataset still perform well in 2023. The study explores the generalization capabilities of these models by evaluating their performance on both the original CoNLL-2003 test set and a newly created CoNLL++ dataset, which includes news articles from 2020 annotated according to the same guidelines. Key findings suggest that while transformer models generally outperform others due to better generalization, larger model sizes also contribute significantly. Additionally, the study identifies temporal drift as the primary cause for performance drops, indicating that models struggle with data from different time periods. The research concludes that for improved generalization, better model architectures, larger model sizes, and more fine-tuning examples are necessary.

Das Vortragende präsentiert ein neues Ansatz zur Python-Codegenerierung, indem es die Interaktivität durch die Fragestellung und Antwort in Form von Clarification Questions (CQs) einführt. Diese Methode zielt darauf ab, die Unterbestimmung von natürlichen Sprachbeschreibungen zu adressieren, indem sie mehr Spezifikationen sammelt. Der Vortrag beschreibt die Einführung einer interaktiven Codegenerierung, die auf der Idee basiert, dass durch die Interaktion mit dem Modell mehr Informationen über die gewünschten Operationen erhoben werden können. Es wird vorgeschlagen, den Codegenerierungsprozess durch die Aufstellung von CQs zu unterstützen, um die Unterbestimmung zu reduzieren. Die Arbeit präsentiert auch einen Dataset namens CodeClarQA, der speziell für die Sammlung von CQs entwickelt wurde, um die Qualität der generierten Codes zu verbessern. Darüber hinaus wird ein Pipeline-Modell vorgestellt, das aus einem Clarification Need Predictor, einem Frageauswahlmodell und einem Codegenerator besteht. Das Modell wird anhand eines synthetischen Datasets getestet und erzielt gute Ergebnisse bei der Identifizierung fehlender Operationen und der Erzeugung von Code.

Was ist kognitive Dissonanz? "Zwei Elemente der Kognition (z.B. Gedanken, Handlungen, Überzeugungen) sind inkonsistent" (Harmon-Jones und Harmon-Jones, 2007)
Eddie Harmon-Jones und Cindy Harmon-Jones, 2007. Cognitive dissonance theory after 50 years of development. Zeitschrift für Sozialpsychologie, 38(1/2), 16.
Kognitive Dissonanz ist die Situation, in der zwei oder mehrere Elemente der Kognition inkonsistent sind. Diese Inkonsistenz führt zu Unbehagen und Druck, um diese Inkonsistenz zu reduzieren. Menschen tendieren dazu, ihre Überzeugungen und Handlungen zu harmonisieren, um kognitive Dissonanz zu vermeiden.
Die Präsentation beschreibt Methoden zur Detektion von Dissonanz in Texten, insbesondere in seltenen Klassen, und wie Transfer- und aktive Lernverfahren dazu beitragen können, die Herausforderung der seltenen Klasse zu meistern. Es wird erklärt, wie kognitive Dissonanz in Sprache ausgedrückt wird und warum sie im Vergleich zu anderen Diskursbeziehungen relativ selten ist. Die Präsentation zeigt auch, wie kognitive Dissonanz Effekte auf Meinungen und Glaubensrichtungen hat und wie sie mit anderen psychologischen Konzepten wie Angststörungen und Extremismus verbunden sein kann.
Es werden verschiedene Strategien vorgestellt, wie man kognitive Dissonanz in Texten detektieren kann, einschließlich der Anwendung von Transfer-Learning und aktiver Lernstrategie. Die Präsentation zeigt, dass Transfer-Learning dazu beitragen kann, die Annahmen von seltenen Klassen zu verbessern, während aktive Lernstrategien helfen, die Annahmen effizienter zu gestalten.

In this research, the team from Carnegie Mellon University introduces CounterComp, a novel approach to enhance compositional generalization for multi-step quantitative reasoning tasks. The study addresses the long-tail issue in compositional generalization, where performance drops significantly with increasing complexity of reasoning steps. CounterComp leverages counterfactual examples derived from questions to improve model performance on both in-distribution and out-of-distribution samples. By focusing on the rate of change between different financial metrics, the method demonstrates superior accuracy compared to existing models across various datasets, including TAT-QA, HitTab, and FinQA. This work not only advances the field of numerical reasoning but also provides practical insights into enhancing machine learning models' ability to handle complex, real-world scenarios.
